questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the procedure giving every member an equal chance of selection
questions.stem: A class wants every student to have an identical chance of being picked. Which procedure is simple random sampling?

options.text: Number every student, then draw names randomly from a full list
Ask for volunteers, then survey whoever steps forward
options.misconception: accepts self-selection as if it were random

options.text: Survey the students seated nearest the front of the room
options.misconception: treats physical convenience as if it were random

options.text: Pick the students whose surnames begin with the letter M
options.misconception: treats a name initial as a random mechanism

questions.explanation: Simple random sampling gives each member a known, equal chance of selection, which numbering and drawing from a complete list guarantees. Volunteering and front-row convenience both over-weight students who are available or nearby, and picking by initial letter takes a systematic slice of the roster rather than a random one.
questions.hint: Look for a mechanism that could produce any name first.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the sampling interval and name the design that uses it
questions.stem: A firm has 1,200 employees listed in hire-date order and must survey exactly 60 of them. Which method takes every twentieth?

options.text: Systematic sampling, with interval k = 1,200/60 = 20 per unit
Simple random sampling, with interval k = 1,200/60 = 20 per unit
options.misconception: labels a fixed-interval walk as a name draw

options.text: Stratified sampling, with interval k = 1,200/60 = 20 per unit
options.misconception: calls a one-per-interval walk a subgroup split

options.text: Cluster sampling, with interval k = 1,200/60 = 20 per unit
options.misconception: calls a fixed-interval walk a whole-group selection

questions.explanation: The interval is k = N/n = 1,200/60 = 20, so taking every twentieth name gives each employee a 1-in-20 chance, which is the definition of systematic sampling. Drawing sixty names at random would be simple random sampling, and a fixed interval walks the roster rather than selecting whole groups, which is what cluster sampling does.
questions.hint: Divide the population by the sample size.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: choose a design that guarantees representation of each subgroup
questions.stem: A researcher needs usable estimates for freshmen, sophomores, juniors, and seniors separately and then combined. Which design fits best?

options.text: Stratified sampling, sampled within each class then reweighted
Systematic sampling, taking every fourth name on the roster
options.misconception: expects per-class guarantees from a fixed interval

options.text: Cluster sampling, choosing four whole classrooms to survey
options.misconception: confuses the sampled subgroup with the sampled units

options.text: Simple random sampling, drawing names from one master list
options.misconception: believes one list alone secures per-class representation

questions.explanation: A stratum is a subgroup that differs internally, so sampling inside each class and reweighting by class size yields per-class estimates plus a valid overall estimate. Choosing whole classrooms is cluster sampling, where the sampled units are groups rather than individuals, and a single random list cannot promise per-class representation.
questions.hint: Decide what gets sampled: people or entire groups.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: recognize a design whose randomly chosen units are whole groups
questions.stem: A state randomly picks 20 of its 400 schools and surveys every student in those 20. Which design is being used?

options.text: Cluster sampling, where the chosen units are whole groups
Stratified sampling, where one student is taken from each school
options.misconception: describes one-per-group as a complete subgroup sample

options.text: Simple random sampling, where all students are equally likely
options.misconception: ignores that every student in a chosen school is taken

options.text: Systematic sampling, where every twentieth school is counted
options.misconception: swaps a random school draw for a fixed interval

questions.explanation: The randomly selected units here are schools, not students, and every member of a chosen cluster is included, which is cluster sampling. One student per school would be stratified sampling, and systematic sampling would follow a fixed interval such as every twentieth school rather than a random draw.
questions.hint: Ask whether a sampled school is fully surveyed or partly surveyed.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify bias created when respondents select themselves
questions.stem: A newspaper asks readers to phone a line to rate a new bus route. Which flaw most threatens that poll?

options.text: Voluntary response bias, since only motivated people phone in
Random sampling error, since the eventual sample size is unknown
options.misconception: labels self-selection as a size-related problem

options.text: Measurement error, since the rating scale has too few points
options.misconception: blames the response scale for a selection problem

options.text: Sampling error, since the line accepts calls for a full week
options.misconception: blames the collection window for self-selection

questions.explanation: Voluntary response bias arises when self-selected respondents differ systematically from the population; riders angry about delays are likelier to call than satisfied riders. An unknown sample size is a planning problem rather than a selection mechanism, and neither the rating scale nor the call window creates the self-selection itself.
questions.hint: Ask who decides to be counted.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: diagnose bias created when refusers differ from repliers
questions.stem: A survey emails 2,000 residents and 800 reply, and the refusers may differ systematically from those who answered. What is the risk?

options.text: Nonresponse bias, since refusers can shift the estimate off target
Coverage bias, since the frame lists addresses that do not exist
options.misconception: calls a reply-rate problem a frame defect

options.text: Response bias, since the questions use double-barrelled wording
options.misconception: calls a participation problem a wording problem

options.text: Clustering error, since the sample was drawn by picking groups
options.misconception: invents a grouping design for a mail survey

questions.explanation: Nonresponse bias appears when people who decline differ on the measured trait from those who answer, and a 60 percent reply rate leaves 1,200 unmeasured whose views may be systematically different. Wording problems are response bias, and nonexistent addresses in the frame would be coverage bias, a different failure at the frame stage.
questions.hint: Decide whether anyone eligible was left unmeasured at the frame stage.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify frame gaps that give some members zero chance of selection
questions.stem: A school surveys only students who own a personal mobile phone, though many families have landlines only. What problem follows?

options.text: Undercoverage, since part of the population has no chance of selection
Voluntary response bias, since students choose to reply or not
options.misconception: turns a frame gap into a decision to participate

options.text: Nonresponse bias, since some invited students skip the form
options.misconception: describes skipping a form nobody with no phone receives

options.text: Response bias, since the survey uses leading question wording
options.misconception: replaces an eligibility problem with a wording problem

questions.explanation: Undercoverage means some members of the target population have zero chance of entering the sample, and students without mobiles are excluded by design rather than by choice. That is a frame problem, not a decision problem, so it differs from voluntary response and nonresponse bias, which both require an opportunity to take part.
questions.hint: Ask whether excluded people were ever offered a chance to be picked.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why easily reached subjects misrepresent a population
questions.stem: A student polls shoppers in one grocery store about a proposed city recycling fee. Which problem most weakens the result?

options.text: Convenience bias, since one store's shoppers are not the city
Random sampling error, since the poll tallied counts by hand
options.misconception: treats a recording method as a sampling defect

options.text: Response bias, since shoppers cannot read the printed question
options.misconception: replaces a selection defect with a reading claim

options.text: Cluster bias, since shoppers arrive in small family groups
options.misconception: treats shoppers' companions as sampled clusters

questions.explanation: Convenience sampling takes whoever is easiest to reach, and shoppers of a single store over-represent that neighborhood's income and shopping habits, so the estimate does not generalize. A hand tally never biases a proportion, and shoppers arriving in groups has no sampling-design consequence at all.
questions.hint: Ask who was easy to reach rather than who was chosen.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify bias introduced by the wording of a question
questions.stem: Two wordings are tested: how useful is the new bus route, and how useless is the new bus route. What flaw does this create?

options.text: Response bias, since leading wording pushes answers one way
Nonresponse bias, since some readers skip the harder phrasing
options.misconception: calls a wording effect a participation effect

options.text: Coverage bias, since the frame omits the nonriders entirely
options.misconception: supplies a frame defect the scenario never mentions

options.text: Sampling error, since the two versions differ in word count
options.misconception: treats phrasing length as a random fluctuation

questions.explanation: Response bias comes from how a question is phrased; reversing a stem from useful to useless tilts the response scale without changing what is measured, so neither version is neutral. Both versions reach the same readers, so nothing is undercovered and nobody is selectively dropping out of the study.
questions.hint: Separate what was measured from how it was asked.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: state the strongest claim an observational study supports
questions.stem: A study logs each student's exercise hours and whether the student scored above 85 percent, assigning nobody. What can it support?

options.text: An association between exercise and high scores, not causation
Proof that raising exercise hours causes higher scores
options.misconception: promotes a correlation to a proven causal claim

options.text: A guarantee the pattern repeats in every future class
options.misconception: turns one cohort result into a universal guarantee

options.text: A causal claim, because every student was actually measured
options.misconception: believes thorough measurement substitutes for randomization

questions.explanation: Because no exercise level was assigned, lurking variables such as prior preparation or sleep could produce the same pattern, so the data support association only. Measuring every student thoroughly is not randomization, and a single cohort's pattern need not repeat in other classes or years.
questions.hint: Ask whether the explanatory variable was imposed by the researcher.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the manipulation that makes a study an experiment
questions.stem: To test a fertilizer claim, a researcher gives fertilizer to half the plots and a look-alike powder to the rest. What makes this an experiment?

options.text: The explanatory variable is manipulated while everything else is held fixed
Existing plots are simply observed and their growth recorded
options.misconception: describes observation as if it were manipulation

options.text: Every plot in the field is sampled before any growth is measured
options.misconception: believes wide coverage creates experimental control

options.text: A correlation between fertilizer amount and plant height is computed
options.misconception: equates a computed correlation with an imposed treatment

questions.explanation: An experiment actively imposes the explanatory variable, so comparing treated and untreated plots isolates its effect on growth. Recording what already happened is an observational study, and a larger or more random sample improves an observation but does not create the manipulation that supports a causal claim.
questions.hint: Look for something the researcher does to the units.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the two randomization procedures and their goals
questions.stem: A class of 30 will be split into two groups of 15 for an experiment. Which step makes that comparison fair?

options.text: Randomly assigning students, so known traits balance by chance
Randomly sampling students from every school in the district
options.misconception: confuses group fairness with population representativeness

options.text: Letting each student pick the group that fits their schedule
options.misconception: believes scheduling choice randomizes the comparison

options.text: Assigning the tallest students to the group given fertilizer
options.misconception: substitutes a known confounder for random allocation

questions.explanation: Random assignment balances both known and unknown traits across groups by chance, so systematic differences become unlikely and any measured gap is attributable to the treatment. Sampling randomly from the whole district targets representativeness for generalization, a separate goal, and self-selection or height-based placement reintroduces confounding.
questions.hint: Ask which purpose you need: fairness now or representativeness later.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose a control group serves in a trial
questions.stem: In a trial of a new antibiotic, half the patients get the drug and half get a placebo. What is the placebo group there for?

options.text: It shows the baseline outcome when no active treatment is given
It ensures every patient in the trial eventually recovers fully
options.misconception: expects the control arm to deliver the outcome

options.text: It doubles the sample size so the results look more impressive
options.misconception: treats group count as a credibility device

options.text: It removes the need to assign patients to groups at random
options.misconception: believes a control arm substitutes for randomization

questions.explanation: The control group estimates the outcome that would occur without the treatment, so improvement in the antibiotic arm is attributed to the drug rather than to natural recovery or expectation. A placebo adds no recovery of its own, and randomization remains essential because the baseline must be comparable.
questions.hint: Ask what would have happened to these patients with no pill at all.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify a third variable that mimics a treatment effect
questions.stem: A survey finds coffee drinkers report more heart palpitations than non-drinkers. What finding would most weaken the causal reading?

options.text: Smokers who are likelier both to drink coffee and to palpitate
The exact cup count recorded for each drinker in the survey
options.misconception: treats precise exposure measurement as a confounder

options.text: The anonymity of the responses, which lowers answering pressure
options.misconception: treats an honesty aid as an alternative cause

options.text: The inclusion of tea drinkers alongside the coffee drinkers
options.misconception: reads a comparison group as a hidden cause

questions.explanation: A confounder is a third variable that tracks both the exposure and the outcome, creating a spurious link; smoking fits because it raises palpitation risk and correlates with coffee intake. Anonymity improves honesty, and precise measurement of cups does not supply an alternative explanation for the association.
questions.hint: Ask what else the two groups differ in besides the exposure.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: state what a placebo control isolates from a treatment
questions.stem: Half the volunteers in a pain study receive sugar pills described as the new medication. Why is that control included?

options.text: It separates the drug's effect from expectation and belief
It reduces how many pills each participant must swallow overall
options.misconception: reduces a logistical detail to the control's purpose

options.text: It guarantees the new drug receives a favorable price point
options.misconception: gives a commercial rationale for a control arm

options.text: It removes the need to measure pain before treatment begins
options.misconception: claims a control replaces a baseline measurement

questions.explanation: A placebo group separates the pharmacological effect of the drug from the expectation that treatment will help, so any difference in reported pain is attributable to the drug. Pill counts, pricing, and the necessity of a baseline measurement are all unaffected by having a placebo arm.
questions.hint: Ask what the sugar pill controls for besides the drug.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: explain how blinding prevents observer expectations from biasing results
questions.stem: Participants rate a solution's smell while the researcher also knows which bottle each came from. How is that bias reduced?

options.text: Blind the researcher to which solution each participant receives
Tell the researcher the results so ratings match expectations
options.misconception: invites the very expectancy bias blinding removes

options.text: Let participants choose their own bottle to raise engagement
options.misconception: removes the control by letting subjects assign treatment

options.text: Ask participants to rate only the solution they expect to like
options.misconception: turns expectancy into the collection rule

questions.explanation: Blinding keeps the observer's expectations from leaking into the ratings, so a researcher who does not know the assignment cannot unconsciously favor one bottle. Sharing results in advance creates exactly the bias blinding removes, and letting subjects or expectations pick the bottle discards the comparison entirely.
questions.hint: Remove the knowledge that could steer the judgement.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: state precisely which error replication reduces and which it cannot
questions.stem: An experiment repeats five times with fresh plants each round and reports the average effect. What does the repetition improve most?

options.text: The effect estimate becomes less disturbed by chance variation
The study becomes observational instead of experimental by design
options.misconception: thinks repeating a design drops the manipulation

options.text: The population of interest is now sampled more completely
options.misconception: claims replication enlarges the target population

options.text: Bias from an unbalanced assignment is eliminated entirely
options.misconception: overstates replication as a bias remedy

questions.explanation: Repeating the design with fresh units and averaging averages out run-to-run noise, tightening the estimate around the true effect. Replication cannot remove selection bias or unbalanced assignment; it reduces random error, and it does not change which population is being sampled.
questions.hint: Separate random error from systematic bias.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the standard error from the spread and sample size
questions.stem: A population has a standard deviation of 20. What is the standard error of the sample mean when n equals 400?

options.misconception: reuses the error for n = 100 by mistake
divides by n instead of by the square root of n
reports the spread itself and skips the division

questions.explanation: The standard error is the spread over the square root of n: 20 / sqrt(400) = 20 / 20 = 1.0. Dividing by n rather than by its square root would give 20/400 = 0.05, and reporting 20.0 forgets to shrink the error at all, which only a larger sample could justify.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the sample size before dividing.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: predict how a fourfold increase in n changes the standard error
questions.stem: A standard error is 4.0. If the sample size grows from 100 to 400 with spread unchanged, what does the error become?

options.misconception: treats the error as proportional to one over n
treats the error as falling by a factor of eight
assumes error is fixed once the spread is fixed

questions.explanation: The standard error equals spread over the square root of n, and sqrt(400)/sqrt(100) = 20/10 = 2, so the error is cut in half: 4.0/2 = 2.0. Treating the error as proportional to 1/n would overstate the gain fourfold, and a fourfold increase in n cannot leave the error untouched.
questions.hint: The square root of 4 is 2, so the error is divided by 2.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Margin of error for a proportion
questions.learningObjective: compute the margin of error for a sample proportion
questions.stem: In a poll of 625 voters, 48 percent support a proposal. At 95 percent confidence, about what is the margin of error?

options.misconception: uses a multiplier of 1 instead of 2
applies the multiplier of 2 twice over
skips the division by the sample size

questions.explanation: The margin of error is about 2 x sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = 2 x sqrt(0.48 x 0.52/625) = 2 x sqrt(0.2496/625) = 2 x sqrt(0.0003994) = 2 x 0.01998, which rounds to 0.040. Halving to 0.020 would use a multiplier of 1, and 0.400 keeps the spread but drops the sample size from the calculation.
questions.hint: Multiply 0.48 by 0.52, divide by 625, then take a root.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: compute a confidence-interval half-width for a sample mean
questions.stem: A sample of 64 has mean 50, drawn from a population with standard deviation 16. What is the 95 percent half-width?

options.misconception: multiplies by the square root of n instead of dividing
omits the 1.96 multiplier on the standard error
squares the standard error instead of using it

questions.explanation: The standard error is 16/sqrt(64) = 16/8 = 2.00, so the half-width is 1.96 x 2.00 = 3.92. Multiplying by the square root would give 124.8, which is backwards because the standard error shrinks as n grows rather than expanding with it.
questions.hint: Find the standard error first, then multiply by 1.96.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: judge the reliability of a proportion estimated from very few observations
questions.stem: A poll of 10 residents finds 6 in favor, giving a reported share of 0.60. Why trust that estimate less?

options.text: With only ten observations the estimate can swing far from truth
With only ten observations the estimate is biased by definition
options.misconception: conflates small-sample variance with selection bias

options.text: With only ten observations the estimate has no sampling error
options.misconception: denies randomness entirely at small n

options.text: With only ten observations the estimate always lands above 0.50
options.misconception: claims a small-n count must exceed one half

questions.explanation: Near a share of 0.5 the standard error is roughly sqrt(0.25/10) = 0.158, so the plausible range around 0.60 runs from about 0.28 to 0.92. Small n widens uncertainty; it does not create bias, since bias comes from how the sample was drawn rather than how large it is.
questions.hint: Compute sqrt of 0.25 over 10 and see how wide it is.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Independence and the five percent rule
questions.learningObjective: decide when observations may be treated as approximately independent
questions.stem: A region holds 2,000,000 residents and a poll takes 400 of them. Why may the 400 answers be treated as independent?

options.text: The sample is 0.02 percent of the population, far under 5 percent
The sample is 2 percent of the population, far under 5 percent
options.misconception: mislocates the decimal when dividing the two counts

options.text: The sample is over 5 percent of the population, so replacement is needed
options.misconception: inflates the share and reverses the conclusion

options.text: The population is 2,000,000, so no adjustment is ever required
options.misconception: grounds the rule in population size alone

questions.explanation: Dividing gives 400 / 2,000,000 = 0.0002, or 0.02 percent, far below the 5 percent guideline, so drawing without replacement barely changes anyone's odds and independence is a safe approximation. The 2 percent figure is off by a factor of 100, and no finite population gives perfect independence.
questions.hint: Compute 400 over 2,000,000 and convert to a percent.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: define the sampling frame and separate it from related constructs
questions.stem: Before drawing a random sample of counties, a researcher needs a list of every county in the state. What is that list?

options.text: The sampling frame, the roster of every eligible element
The sampling distribution, the pattern across many samples
options.misconception: equates the source list with the result pattern

options.text: The parameter space, all values the estimate could take
options.misconception: reads a list of units as a list of numbers

options.text: The confidence interval, the range holding the true value
options.misconception: names an interval estimate as the sampling source

questions.explanation: The sampling frame is the operational roster of the population, so the list of counties is the frame and the random draw selects from it. A sampling distribution describes what repeated samples produce, a parameter space is not a roster of units, and a confidence interval is an interval estimate rather than a source list.
questions.hint: Which term names the list the random draw works from?

questions.learningObjective: recognize bias from conditioning the sample on an outcome
questions.stem: A comfort survey interviews only passengers who were uninjured in three emergency landings. Which bias does that create?

options.text: Survivorship bias, since the sample excludes the worst affected
Voluntary response bias, since passengers chose to be interviewed
options.misconception: invents a choice the scenario never offered

options.text: Nonresponse bias, since some passengers declined the interview
options.misconception: invents refusals among the uninjured only

options.text: Undercoverage bias, since the frame omitted whole airlines
options.misconception: supposes an airline-level frame gap unmentioned

questions.explanation: Conditioning the sample on having survived selects on the outcome itself, so the interviewed group is systematically milder than the population of all passengers and comfort looks better than it is. questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: explain how pooled rates can reverse subgroup comparisons
questions.stem: Group A beats group B on recovery overall, yet inside every age band group B recovers at a higher rate. What is happening?

options.text: The pooled rates average over groups with different case mixes
The band-level rates came from samples of exactly equal size
options.misconception: claims equal sizes, which would prevent a reversal

options.text: The pooled rates were computed after every value was reweighted
options.misconception: invents a reweighting that removes the reversal

options.text: The band-level rates used a different outcome than the totals
options.misconception: reaches for a measurement mismatch instead of weighting

questions.explanation: A pooled comparison can reverse because the group with the better band-level rates may be made up mostly of low-risk members; pooling then compares different case mixes rather than treatments. questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: match a sampling fix to the specific defect it repairs
questions.stem: To reach people who only use mobiles, a poller dials random numbers that reach both lines. What does that repair?

options.text: Undercoverage, since both kinds of telephone line are reachable
Nonresponse, since interviewers are trained to be brief
options.misconception: credits dialing method with response improvement

options.text: Response bias, since questions are rewritten in neutral wording
options.misconception: credits dialing method with wording improvement

options.text: Sampling error, since many more calls are placed overall
options.misconception: credits dialing method with a size reduction

questions.explanation: The defect being repaired is frame coverage: a landline-only frame cannot reach mobile-only households, and random-digit dialing across both line types removes that gap. questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: identify claims that go beyond the sampled population
questions.stem: A poll surveys residents of one coastal city and reports the outcome as the opinion of the whole country. What is wrong?

options.text: Overgeneralization, since the sample cannot stand for the nation
Undercoverage, since the frame omitted the city's residents
options.misconception: claims the sampled people were left out

options.text: Nonresponse bias, since many city residents skipped the form
options.misconception: invents refusals in a completed survey

options.text: Measurement error, since opinions were recorded without a scale
options.misconception: attacks the recording device, not the claim

questions.explanation: Overgeneralization applies a result beyond the population actually sampled; a single coastal city is not the nation, so the claim outruns the frame rather than breaking it. questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: choose the design that corrects an unbalanced subgroup response rate
questions.stem: One district returns 80 percent of its questionnaires and a second returns 20 percent. Which design best protects accuracy?

options.text: Stratifying by district, oversampling the weaker district
Simple random sampling, drawing names from a combined list
options.misconception: lets the eager district dominate a pooled draw

options.text: Voluntary response sampling, using whoever returns a form
options.misconception: formalizes the imbalance that needs correcting

options.text: Convenience sampling, using only the higher-returning district
options.misconception: hard-codes the very imbalance under repair

questions.explanation: Stratifying by district and oversampling the low-response district corrects the imbalance, because a random draw from a combined list would be dominated by the eager district. Voluntary response and convenience sampling both formalize the imbalance rather than repairing it, so the overall estimate stays skewed.
questions.hint: Pick the design that controls how many come from each district.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: compare precision of two designs with equal total sample size
questions.stem: Two surveys of identical total size cost the same: one draws individuals at random, one draws whole classrooms. What differs?

options.text: Cluster sampling usually shows more variability than individual draws
Cluster sampling usually shows less variability than individual draws
options.misconception: assumes grouped units behave like independent ones

options.text: Both show identical variability whenever the total size matches
options.misconception: assumes equal counts imply equal information

options.text: Cluster sampling shows less variability only with equal cluster sizes
options.misconception: ties precision to cluster size rather than independence

questions.explanation: Whole-cluster sampling takes many units that share one local circumstance, so neighbors are effectively counted repeatedly and the effective sample size falls below the nominal total, raising variability. Matching totals does not restore independence, and equal cluster sizes change the weighting rather than removing the correlation.
questions.hint: Ask how much truly independent information the sample contains.
